---
title: "Evaluation"
description: "Measure a function on rows with known answers: a score with its interval, a table of every answer, and paired comparisons."
---

{{< include ../_setup.qmd >}}

A prompt that looks right on three examples can be wrong on the fourth.
The only way to know how well a function works is to run it on examples
with known answers and count. `functai.evaluate` does that, and gives you
the score *with its uncertainty*, and every answer as a table to dig
into.

Tables come from [dpyr](https://github.com/MaximeRivest/dpyr) (dplyr's
verbs, in Python, over polars and duckdb): `pip install "functai[data]"`.

## Data is rows

A list of dictionaries, or any table: a CSV or parquet file, a pandas or
polars dataframe, a Hugging Face dataset. Columns named like the
function's **parameters** are its inputs. A column named like an
**output** is the expected answer (`result` for the return value). Any
other column is kept, to group or filter by later.

The support desk from [Get started](../get-started.qmd) routes each
message to a team. It has two house rules the model can't guess: an item
that arrives broken is a **shipping** claim (the carrier pays), and
anything about money back is **billing**.

```{python}
from typing import Literal

@ai
def category(message: str) -> Literal["shipping", "billing", "product", "account"]:
    """The support category of the message."""

dev = [
    {"message": "The mug arrived in pieces.",                          "result": "shipping", "channel": "email"},
    {"message": "I want my money back for the toaster, it's useless.", "result": "billing",  "channel": "chat"},
    {"message": "The kettle's lid doesn't close properly.",            "result": "product",  "channel": "email"},
    {"message": "How do I change the email on my profile?",            "result": "account",  "channel": "chat"},
    {"message": "Box was crushed and the lamp inside is cracked.",     "result": "shipping", "channel": "email"},
    {"message": "Please refund the blender, it stopped working.",      "result": "billing",  "channel": "chat"},
    {"message": "Toaster burns one side of the bread.",                "result": "product",  "channel": "chat"},
    {"message": "Please delete my account and my data.",               "result": "account",  "channel": "email"},
    {"message": "Screen was shattered when I opened the package.",     "result": "shipping", "channel": "chat"},
    {"message": "Return the headphones and give me a refund please.",  "result": "billing",  "channel": "email"},
    {"message": "Tracking hasn't moved in a week.",                    "result": "shipping", "channel": "email"},
    {"message": "My coupon code didn't apply at checkout.",            "result": "billing",  "channel": "chat"},
]
```

## A score, and how sure it is

```{python}
ev = functai.evaluate(category, dev, num_threads=8)
ev
```

With no metric given, the score is exact match against the `result`
column (ignoring case and spacing). **The interval is the part to
read.** On 12 examples the true accuracy could be anywhere in it; on 30
examples, 80% still means "somewhere between 63% and 90%". Collect more
examples before you trust a small difference.

`ev.summary` has one row per metric:

```{python}
ev.summary
```

## Every answer, as a table

`ev.table` has one row per example: the data, the prediction
(`pred_result`), each metric, the error if the row failed, the time and
the tokens it took. Because it is a table, the usual data tools apply.
The misses:

```{python}
from dpyr import col, n

ev.table.filter(col.exact_match == 0).select(col.message, col.result, col.pred_result)
```

Exactly the house rules: the model files broken items under *product*,
and refunds under whatever they are about. Accuracy by category, and by
the channel the message came from:

```{python}
ev.table.group_by(col.result).summarize(accuracy=col.exact_match.mean(), n=n())
```

```{python}
ev.table.group_by(col.channel).summarize(accuracy=col.exact_match.mean())
```

`ev.write("today.parquet")` saves it; `ev.table.collect()` gives a polars
dataframe.

## Metrics

A metric scores one row. It can be:

- **a function** `metric(row, prediction) -> float | bool`: the row as a
  dict, the prediction with attribute access;
- **a dpyr expression** over the table's columns, computed on the whole
  table at once: `col.pred_result == col.result`;
- **an AI function**, acting as a judge (one model call per row). Use a
  judge when "right" can't be checked by code: a summary, a translation,
  a reply's tone.

Give several as a dict; the first is the one `ev.score` reports.

```{python}
@ai
def plausible(row: dict, prediction: dict) -> float:
    """Between 0 and 1: could a reasonable support agent have chosen the
    predicted category for this message, even if it is not the expected one?"""

ev2 = functai.evaluate(category, dev, {
    "exact": col.pred_result == col.result,
    "not_account": lambda row, pred: pred.result != "account",
    "plausible": plausible,
}, num_threads=8)
ev2.summary
```

A row whose run fails (a provider error, an unreadable reply) keeps its
message in the `error` column; its metrics are null in the table and
count 0 in the score. Problems that would waste a whole run (a missing
input column, a metric with the wrong signature) are refused before any
model is called.

## Comparing two versions

The misses showed the model doesn't know the house rules, so state them
in the docstring, and compare the two versions **on the same examples**.
`compare` pairs them row by row, which detects a real change with far
fewer examples than two separate scores would:

```{python}
@ai
def category_v2(message: str) -> Literal["shipping", "billing", "product", "account"]:
    """The support category of the message.
    House rules: an item that arrived broken is shipping (the carrier pays),
    and any request for money back is billing."""

after = functai.evaluate(category_v2, dev, num_threads=8)
functai.compare(ev, after)
```

`better`, `worse` and `same` count examples that changed. `low` and
`high` bound the difference: when they include 0, the change could be
luck, and the honest next step is more examples.

## Keeping a record

`evaluate(..., log="runs/")` writes each run to `runs/<run>.parquet`, and
`functai.runs("runs/")` reads all of them back as one table: every
version you tried, side by side.
